title: System State Backup and Recovery Point Discipline for Domain Controllers
summary: Build an operationally safe AD recovery posture by understanding what System State protects, how to create it, and why backup age and trust matter during recovery.
objective: Explain the role of System State in DC recovery, identify a trusted recovery point, and separate backup creation from the much higher-risk act of restoring a production domain controller.
body_outline: Microsoft documents System State backup for domain controllers on Windows Server 2025, 2022, 2019 and 2016 using Windows Server Backup or wbadmin.

A recovery plan must identify not only a technically valid backup but the last trusted backup before corruption or compromise; restoring a newer but compromised backup defeats the purpose of recovery.
Backup currency defines the recovery point: changes after the selected backup can be lost during forest recovery.
Backup creation is routine protection; restoration is an incident-controlled operation that must account for DSRM credentials, isolation, replication state and the recovery scenario.
quick_check: Why can the newest available domain-controller backup still be the wrong recovery point during a compromise?

title: AD Backup in Plain English: Save a Trusted Checkpoint
summary: A useful AD backup is a trusted checkpoint you can return to, not merely the newest copy on disk.
analogy: Think of a backup like a save point in a game. If the save was made after the game state became corrupted, loading the newest save simply restores the corruption too.
plain_language_explanation: System State gives you recovery material for a domain controller, but the recovery team still has to decide which backup is known-good. Age, compromise timing, replication health and documented change history all matter.
visual_hint: Timeline showing healthy state, compromise point, multiple backups and the last trusted backup selected for recovery.
quick_check: Is the newest backup automatically the safest backup to restore?

title: Authoritative vs Nonauthoritative AD Restore: Choosing the Correct Replication Semantics
summary: Understand how restored directory data rejoins replication and why authoritative restore must be narrowly scoped to the objects that must win against newer replicas.
architecture_notes: A nonauthoritative restore rebuilds the local AD DS state from backup and then allows newer replicated directory state to converge from replication partners. An authoritative restore deliberately marks selected restored objects so their restored versions are replicated outward as the versions that should win.
internals: Microsoft guidance distinguishes system-state restoration from authoritative restoration. Ntdsutil authoritative restore targets object or subtree distinguished names; narrower object-level scope reduces the number of unrelated attributes and objects rolled back to backup-era values.
failure_modes: Using an authoritative restore too broadly can roll back valid post-backup password, membership, profile, location, contact, and security-descriptor changes. Using a nonauthoritative restore when the intent is to recover accidentally deleted objects can allow newer deletion state from partners to win again.
trade_offs: Object-level authoritative restore is more precise but operationally slower for large sets. Subtree restore is faster for a tightly bounded affected OU but has a larger rollback blast radius.
enterprise_design_notes: Treat restore scope as a change-control decision with explicit object inventory and replication plan. Forest recovery and isolated first-DC recovery remain distinct from routine recovery of a bounded deletion incident.

title: Create and Validate a Domain Controller System State Backup
summary: Create a System State backup in an isolated lab, document its recovery metadata, and validate that the backup is visible before any restore drill is attempted.
objective: Produce a restorable lab System State backup and capture the evidence needed to judge its suitability for a future recovery drill.
prerequisites_detail: Disposable or controlled lab domain controller, sufficient backup storage, Windows Server Backup feature available, and no production restore activity.
environment: Single lab DC or isolated test DC running a supported Windows Server version.
topology: Lab DC -> dedicated backup target; no recovery operation is performed in this exercise.
steps: Record DC identity, OS version, current time, replication health and the intended backup target.
Create a System State backup using Windows Server Backup or the Microsoft-documented wbadmin workflow for the lab environment.
Confirm the backup job completed successfully and record backup time, version identifier and storage location.
List available backups and verify the newly created recovery point is discoverable.
Document whether this backup predates or postdates any intentionally simulated configuration changes so the restore point can be selected intelligently in a later drill.
expected_result: The backup completes without error and appears in the available backup-version inventory with a recorded timestamp and target.
validation: Cross-check the backup timestamp against the lab change log and retain evidence sufficient to identify the recovery point without starting a restore.
rollback: No restore is performed. If the backup target was temporary, remove only the test backup after evidence capture and according to lab retention policy.
cleanup: Do not delete the only usable lab recovery point if a later restore drill depends on it.

title: Deleted AD Object: Recycle Bin, Nonauthoritative Restore, or Authoritative Restore?
summary: Use a bounded recovery decision tree to choose the least disruptive supported recovery path for deleted directory objects.
symptoms: One or more users, computers or groups were deleted
A restored DC receives deletion state again after replication
Recovery team is unsure whether to restore an object or an entire OU subtree
diagnostic_order: Define the exact affected objects and confirm whether the incident is deletion-only or part of broader corruption/compromise.
Check whether Active Directory Recycle Bin provides a supported lower-impact recovery path for the affected objects.
If backup-based recovery is required, identify the last trusted backup containing the objects.
Choose the narrowest authoritative scope that meets the recovery objective; prefer exact objects or the lowest common affected container rather than a broad unrelated subtree.
Plan outbound replication and post-restore validation before executing any authoritative recovery.
evidence_to_capture: group membership and security descriptor expectations
escalation_boundary: Do not run ntdsutil authoritative restore commands against production solely from a helpdesk symptom. Recovery requires an approved incident/change path, trusted backup selection and explicit object scope.

title: OU Design and Delegation as a Least-Privilege Control Plane
summary: Design OU ownership and delegated administration so routine account/resource management does not require domain-wide service-admin privileges.
objective: Design an OU/delegation model that separates service administration from data administration and limits delegated rights to the smallest practical subtree and task set.
body_outline: Microsoft distinguishes account OUs containing users, groups and computers from resource OUs containing resources and the accounts used to manage them.
The forest owner creates the OU structure and delegates control to OU owners or data administrators rather than granting broad domain administrative membership.
Delegation should align with business ownership and operational tasks: create/reset/manage only the object classes and child OUs required by the role.

Default and sensitive containers, privileged groups and the Domain Controllers OU require tighter service-administrator control; delegation should not become a shortcut around privileged-tier boundaries.
quick_check: Why is placing a support team in Domain Admins usually the wrong solution when they only need to manage user objects in one business OU?

title: AD Recovery and Delegated Administration Checkpoint
summary: Scenario assessment covering trusted backups, restore semantics, recovery scope and least-privilege OU delegation.

assessment_items.question: A compromise began Monday and backups exist from Sunday, Tuesday and Wednesday. Which backup is the first recovery candidate and why?
assessment_items.answer: Sunday is the first candidate because it predates the known compromise; the newest backup is not automatically trusted.

assessment_items.question: When would an authoritative restore be preferred over a nonauthoritative restore?
assessment_items.answer: When selected restored objects must become the versions replicated outward rather than being superseded by newer partner state, such as a bounded deleted-object recovery from backup.

assessment_items.question: Why should authoritative restore target the narrowest practical DN scope?
assessment_items.answer: Broader scope can roll back unrelated valid object and attribute changes to their backup-era values.

assessment_items.question: A regional support team only manages users in one regional OU. What is the safer privilege model?
assessment_items.answer: Delegate only the required user-management permissions on that OU rather than granting domain-wide administrative group membership.

title: Senior AD Engineer Interview: Recovery Scope and Delegation Trade-offs
summary: Senior-level scenarios testing judgement around trusted restore points, restore blast radius and delegated administration.

questions.question: How would you choose between Recycle Bin, authoritative object restore, subtree restore and forest recovery after an AD incident?
answer_points: prefer the least disruptive supported recovery mechanism
use the last trusted backup when backup recovery is required
authoritatively restore only the necessary object/container scope
reserve forest recovery for forest-wide failure or compromise

questions.question: How would you give a service desk password-reset rights without making it a privileged domain administrator?
answer_points: delegate only required rights to a dedicated group
audit membership and delegated ACL changes
